title: AI for wireless communications and healthcare research at Kyung Hee University
abstract: Professors at Kyung Hee University connect artificial intelligence, communications and quantum science with clinical and industrial partners. In this Viewpoint, four professors discuss how uniting intelligence initiatives with trauma centres in healthcare, quantum computing and 6G technologies improves predictive models for patient outcomes.

title: Accelerating the semiconductor innovation pipeline
authors: Cesar Javier Lockhart de la Rosa
abstract: The growth of artificial intelligence requires better computation at lower energy. Semiconductors remain the more prolific materials platform driving practical improvements to device hardware. Here, the authors outline a critical pathway for accelerating the transfer of early findings in material science into manufactural processes for faster scale-up and technology applications.

title: The heterogeneous integration of electronic components
abstract: Heterogeneous integration (HI) of electronics components is broadly recognized as a powerful and crucial enabler for the continued growth of computing and communication. From 2010 onwards, the value of HI is increasingly visible in the advanced packaging used in artificial intelligence, high-performance computing, smartphones and communications product implementations. In this Perspective, we argue that HI is crucial to semiconductors and more broadly to the continued evolution of computing and communications. We use leading-edge advanced packaging examples to represent the value, advancements and opportunities for HI. To succeed, it is critical to develop comprehensive HI roadmaps that inform collaborations across the design, manufacturing and reliability spectrum between systems architects, packaging and semiconductor technologists to common goals. Although this article does not provide a full roadmap, we instead detail additional parameters for artificial intelligence, smartphone and other cellular communication devices, and their constituent building blocks including interconnects, power electronics, photonics, thermal management, reliability, modelling and co-design, to foster greater collaboration opportunities among academia, research laboratories and industry.

title: Quantum computing for smart grid
abstract: Smart grids are under a new kind of computational pressure. As renewable penetration, decentralization and digitalization deepen, design and scheduling problems turn combinatorial, modelling becomes multiphysics across timescales from nanoseconds to years and fault diagnostics must work from very few labelled examples. These shifts stretch the classical simulation, optimization and control workflows used at the converter and grid levels. In this Review, we ask where quantum computing could ease those bottlenecks. We treat the two levels together, because they expose the same family of difficulties and match the same family of quantum approaches — simulation, optimization, machine learning and security. Across four converter-level and five grid-level tasks, we identify where quantum approaches have a credible near-term role inside otherwise classical workflows and where they do not yet fit. We close with the shared technical and ecosystem barriers and a staged roadmap towards quantum-enabled smart grids.

title: Quantum sensing and intelligent imaging research at Daegu Gyeongbuk Institute of Science and Technology
abstract: Electrical engineering research at Daegu Gyeongbuk Institute of Science and Technology (DGIST) integrates physical AI, human digital twin and quantum sensing with advanced semiconductor fabrication and quantum-dot optoelectronics, translating innovation in nanoscale materials into scalable sensing and imaging technologies for next-generation intelligent systems.

title: Engineering topolectrical circuits
abstract: Topolectrical circuits are electrical networks that encode topological band theory. Their physical behaviour is set by how the components are wired together, not by where they are placed. This wiring-centred design delivers defect tolerance, directional signal flow without bulky magnetic parts, and amplified response at boundaries. Conventional electronics obtain these only by adding isolators, feedback or calibration after the circuit is laid out. In this Review, we identify which capabilities are engineering-ready and which remain confined to the laboratory. We cover the underlying physics, the resulting sensors and engineering applications, and cross-disciplinary uses in quantum simulation, artificial intelligence-assisted design and curved-space geometries. We then examine how co-integration with memristive devices makes the platform adaptive and history-dependent. We close with the hardware routes towards deployable electronics, from monolithic chips to flexible substrates and body-worn systems.

title: Building digital twin brains at the limits of measurement
abstract: The brain remains among the hardest systems in biology to model. Whole-brain simulations, neuromorphic systems and predictive surrogates are among the main approaches, but each captures isolated aspects of brain function rather than a specific living brain that can be updated over time. Digital twin brains (DTBs) reframe the goal as individualized, data-coupled models for which structure and dynamics are constrained by subject-specific measurements. In this Review, we argue that the fidelity a DTB can reach is set by the resolution, completeness and updatability of those measurements, not by neuron count — a measurement-defined emulation scale. On this scale, today’s DTBs are best understood as partial, simulation-based counterparts: they reconstruct structure and reproduce dynamics, yet persistent updating, closed-loop interaction and embodiment remain long-term goals. Building DTBs at biological scale will depend as much on data integration, validation and governance as on raw computation. DTBs are therefore emerging as instruments for health care, discovery and brain-inspired artificial intelligence.

title: Autonomous driving chips
abstract: The automobile is undergoing a dramatic transformation — from a conventional mode of transportation to an intelligent, interconnected terminal within the Internet of Everything. As driving functions progressively shift from human drivers to onboard AI systems, vehicles are becoming intelligent agents operating in complex, safety-critical environments. In this transition, autonomous driving chips are emerging as a key determinant of whether safe, scalable and commercially viable autonomy can be achieved. We argue that the future of autonomous driving will be shaped by a widening gap between rapidly growing computational demands and the physical limits of conventional chip technologies. Closing this gap requires a paradigm shift from isolated hardware or software innovation towards holistic hardware–software codesign. This Perspective examines how increasingly stringent requirements for safety, real-time intelligence and cost are reshaping the design of autonomous driving chips, and discusses the challenges of sustaining performance growth as conventional scaling approaches slow down. Particular attention is given to emerging opportunities in advanced materials, logic and memory technologies, heterogeneous monolithic three-dimensional integration and domain-specific architectures. By connecting developments across semiconductor technology and autonomous driving algorithms, we discuss the key technological bottlenecks, design trade-offs and cross-disciplinary innovations that are likely to shape the next generation of intelligent computing platforms for autonomous systems.

title: Towards system-level artificial intelligence in perovskite photovoltaics
abstract: Halide perovskite solar cells (PSCs) offer tunable optoelectronic properties and low fabrication costs; however, their industrial deployment is constrained by tightly coupled dependencies among composition, processing and device architecture. Artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely applied across the PSC research cycle, but its impact remains uneven: models accelerate local optimization within data-rich regimes yet do not generalize across compositions, fabrication environments or device architectures. This unevenness reflects the difficulty of representing the coupled, cross-scale relationships that govern PSC behaviour rather than a limitation of modelling capability alone. We examine AI applications across materials discovery, device engineering, process optimization and stability analysis, identify four structural bottlenecks (fragmented data, weak generalization, limited interpretability and misaligned design objectives) and outline research directions to address each. Broad impact will require a transition from task-specific predictive tools towards system-level AI integration that preserves knowledge across the PSC research cycle.

title: Multimodal semantic communications
abstract: Multimodal semantic communication focuses on transmitting meaning of multimodal data rather than exact bits or symbols. By exploiting semantic correlations and complementarities across modalities, it supports reliable transmission under extremely poor conditions and severely limited bandwidth. For instance, it remains effective under 0-dB signal-to-noise ratio and with only a few kilohertz of available spectrum. These properties make multimodal semantic communication attractive for applications that involve massive multimodal data and tight spectrum constraints, such as immersive communication and satellite networks. In this Review, we clarify the distinction between multimedia communication and multimodal communication, revealing a shift from independent data processing towards joint semantic understanding across modalities. Here, semantic theories provide quantitative metrics for semantic communication and core methods in multimodal semantic communication allow practical approaches to process and transmit multimodal semantics. Deep learning-based representation, sampling, coding, modulation and resource allocation methods enable efficient and reliable multimodal semantic communication systems. Finally, we outline a unified, green and compatible multimodal semantic communication to support intelligent connectivity for humans and agents.

title: Transferable predictive maintenance for battery energy storage systems
abstract: Battery energy storage systems are becoming multi-role infrastructures whose functions extend beyond energy storage and keep evolving over long deployment horizons. This evolution drives persistent operational drift in application requirements, duty cycles, environmental exposure and monitoring pipelines, whereas predictive maintenance still largely assumes fixed roles and stationary conditions. Drift therefore undermines the reliability of predictive maintenance, compromising system safety, asset availability and operational resilience. This Perspective proposes a system-level framework for transferable predictive maintenance under structured operational drift. We classify the sources of operational drift across evolving asset roles and organize their effects into layered functional mismatches spanning data, model and temporal layers. Each mismatch layer is linked to targeted transfer strategies, which we assess against negative transfer, catastrophic forgetting, calibrated uncertainty and sample efficiency. We position transferable predictive maintenance as a life-cycle-spanning capability connecting manufacturing, first-life operation and second-life deployment and outline the data infrastructures, foundation models, open benchmarks and regulatory recommendations needed to sustain it.

title: Unlocking battery boundaries
abstract: Chuying Ouyang, vice president of Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited (CATL) and executive deputy director of its 21C Innovation Laboratory, shares his excitement about advancing systems engineering and discusses how systems engineering pushes battery performance to its limits, and how artificial intelligence (AI) and electrical engineering together are reshaping energy storage. Materials define the fundamental boundaries of battery performance, and systems engineering is how the industry will unlock them, says Chuying Ouyang, vice president of CATL. He talks ultra-fast charging, AI already working in factories and why electrical engineers underestimate how designable batteries really are.

title: Probabilistic algorithms for Ising machines from optimization to generative AI
abstract: Ising machines have emerged as promising hardware accelerators for intractable optimization and sampling problems, yet their practical impact increasingly hinges on the co-design of algorithms and hardware, in which algorithmic demands shape new architectures, and new hardware capabilities inspire entirely new algorithms. In this Review, we survey probabilistic algorithms designed for portability across diverse Ising platforms, advocating a top-down perspective that prioritizes principled methods with provable guarantees. We cover foundational methods such as simulated annealing and parallel tempering, including two-dimensional extensions that natively encode hard constraints, and examine approaches that expand the scale of solvable problems from cluster mean-field methods to variational samplers. We highlight the Probabilistic Approximate Optimization Algorithm, a classical analogue of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm that emerged directly from probabilistic hardware development, and explore how generative AI and Ising machines might reinforce each other: learned models propose global moves to accelerate optimization and probabilistic techniques improve inference in large language models. Much as quantum computing has seen algorithms co-evolve with hardware, probabilistic and Ising computing stand at a similar inflection point. We outline a co-design framework for accelerating the capabilities and adoption of next-generation Ising machines.
keywords: Statistical physics, thermodynamics and nonlinear dynamics

title: Three-dimensional dynamic random-access memory beyond two-dimensional scaling limits
abstract: Dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) technology has advanced through scaling and cell structure innovations to enhance performance and density. However, moving to sub-10-nm nodes raises concerns about the scalability and long-term viability of 2D architectures. In this Review we examine the evolution of 2D DRAMs and explain how the integration strategies of cell-stacked 3D DRAM can overcome the scaling limitations of conventional structures, distinct from chip-stacked high-bandwidth memory. Two-dimensional DRAM faces many challenges, including capacitor limitations, high word-line resistance and row-hammer effects. Thus, 3D DRAM necessitates circuit and structural innovations such as vertical bit-line designs, gate-all-around transistors and innovative channel materials such as single-crystal silicon and amorphous oxide semiconductors. However, process challenges, including staircase word-line contacts and wafer bonding hinder the realization of scaled 3D DRAM. Although many integration hurdles remain, 3D DRAM is poised to become a crucial enabler for next-generation artificial intelligence computing.
